title: Can an affected person actually obtain human review before an automated adverse decision takes effect?
description: A board-level oversight question testing whether an organization's automated decision-making systems provide genuine pre-decision human review, rather than only a theoretical or post-hoc appeals right.

history.note: Normalized US/UK spelling variants to the American-English house style (schema field names, e.g. organizations_involved, are already American; majority framework citations - NIST, FTC, EEOC, FCRA, BIPA - are American sources).

question_text: For every automated system we use that can adversely affect a person's benefits eligibility, education outcome, or similar legal rights, can that person obtain meaningful human review of the specific decision before it takes effect — and do we have a completed data protection impact assessment showing we thought about this before deployment, not after harm was reported?
rationale: The Dutch SyRI/childcare-benefits scandal, the UK Ofqual grading algorithm, and Australia's Robodebt scheme each involved an automated system making or heavily informing an adverse decision with no genuine human-review safeguard before the decision took effect — in each case, the harm was only corrected after significant public and legal pressure.
follow_up_actions: Request the current data protection impact assessment for every in-scope automated decision system.
Confirm the human-review step happens before the adverse decision takes effect, not only via a later appeal.
Ask whether the system has been classified against relevant high-risk categories and what that classification implied for safeguards.
